opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is something people underestimate. When we started building evals, the hard part was mostly intellectual: what's a good question, how do you grade it, does it capture the capability you care about? That's still hard, but as models get more capable, the tasks we want to measure get much longer and messier.

If you want to know whether a model can do real economically valuable work, like the job of a lawyer, an engineer, or a financial analyst, you can't just write a multiple-choice question. You need actual experts in those fields to design realistic tasks, and you need them to grade the outputs, which might be a long report or a codebase or a full project that took hours to produce. Finding those people, paying them, making sure they agree with each other, and running that at scale is a big operational lift.

Then there's the infrastructure side. Agentic tasks need environments: computers, software, sometimes access to tools or websites, and they have to be reproducible so you're comparing models fairly. A single eval run might take hours per task instead of seconds. Multiply that across many tasks and many model versions and it becomes a real logistics problem.

So I think the frontier of evaluation is shifting from "can we think of a clever benchmark" to "can we actually run something that resembles real work, reliably and at scale." The teams that figure out the operations, recruiting experts, building environments, managing grading pipelines, are the ones who'll be able to tell us what these models can actually do. And honestly, that's increasingly where the bottleneck is.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the thing people don't fully appreciate is that evaluating a model used to be really cheap. You'd have a benchmark, maybe a few thousand multiple-choice questions, and you'd just run the model over it and get a number. That takes minutes. It's basically free.

But the models have gotten good enough that those kinds of tests are saturated. If you want to know what GPT-5 or whatever the next model is can actually do, you have to test it on things that look like real work. And real work is messy. It takes hours or days, not seconds. It involves tools, environments, other people, sometimes physical stuff.

So take something like evaluating whether a model can do the work of a software engineer, or a lawyer, or a research scientist. To even build that eval, you need actual experts to write the tasks, and then you need other experts to grade the outputs, because there's often no single right answer. A lot of our evals now involve hundreds of domain professionals, and coordinating that is a logistics problem more than a machine learning problem. You're recruiting people, writing contracts, building grading rubrics, resolving disagreements between graders, making sure nobody leaks the tasks. None of that scales the way running a script scales.

And then on the compute side, if a task takes a model eight hours of agentic work, and you want to run it enough times to get a statistically meaningful result, across multiple models, you're talking about a lot of wall-clock time and a lot of infrastructure. Sandboxes, environments that reset cleanly, ways to intervene if something goes sideways. That's all operational muscle.

So I think the capability of the models will keep going up, but our ability to measure it is going to be gated by how fast we can build these elaborate, human-in-the-loop, long-horizon test setups. The science of what to measure is hard, but honestly the harder part is increasingly just getting the measurement done.

r001.rationale: The response says realistic evaluations involve tools and environments, and describes long-running agentic tasks that need sandboxes and resettable environments. This connects the evaluation burden to agents working in external environments.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention delegating programming to Codex or a resulting shift in Tejal Patwardhan’s work toward operations.

astra-6.text:
I think as models get more capable, the tasks we need to give them to measure those capabilities become longer and more complicated. If a model can answer a question in a few seconds, it’s relatively easy to run that test and check the answer. But if you want to know whether it can do a project that would take a person several days, you need a realistic environment, the right tools and data, and a clear way to judge whether it succeeded.

And then you have to do that repeatedly. You need people who can design those tasks, experts who can evaluate the results, and infrastructure that can support long runs without something unrelated breaking. If a run fails, you have to figure out whether that tells you something about the model or whether the environment was misconfigured.

So the bottleneck starts to shift from asking the model a hard question to organizing a reliable test of meaningful work. We may have models that can do things before we have the operational capacity to measure those abilities well.

sol-6.1.text:
I think as models get more capable, measuring what they can do starts to look less like giving them a test and more like setting up a real project. You need a realistic environment, the right tools and data, and experts who can tell whether the result is actually good. And if the task takes hours or days, you need to keep that whole setup running reliably.

So the bottleneck becomes coordinating all of that. Can you get enough expert time? Can you run enough trials to distinguish a reliable capability from a lucky success? When something fails, was it the model, or was the environment broken? Those are operational questions, but they directly affect what you can conclude about the model. The ability to build and run good evaluations may end up moving more slowly than the capabilities we’re trying to measure.
